2027-06-20.title: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles

readings: The commandments of the Lord give life
All the nations shall stream to the mountain of the Lord
Do everything for the glory of God

2027-06-20.alt: Season of the Apostles (Šleehe), which began at Pentecost: the Church remembers how the apostles, filled with the Holy Spirit, carried the Gospel to the nations and founded the Churches. The Holy Qurbana is celebrated with the Anaphora of Addai and Mari, and since Pentecost the Angel of the Lord (Angelus) is prayed in place of the Queen of Heaven. The calendar gives longer forms: Deuteronomy 4:1–10; Isaiah 2:1–19; 1 Corinthians 10:14–32; Luke 12:57–13:17 (with the parable of the barren fig tree and the healing of the bent woman on the sabbath). In the Latin calendar today is the Twelfth Sunday in Ordinary Time.
2027-06-20.verse: No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all perish as they did.
theo: Five weeks after Pentecost the readings of the Season of the Apostles put a question to us: what does it look like to live as God's people in the middle of the nations? The first reading answers from the plains of Moab. Moses, about to die, gathers Israel at the edge of the promised land: “So now, Israel, give heed to the statutes and ordinances that I am teaching you to observe, so that you may live to enter and occupy the land”. Notice the purpose: so that you may live. God's commandments are not a fence around our happiness but the shape of life itself. “You must neither add anything to what I command you nor take away anything from it”: neither the religion that piles up human rules nor the religion that quietly drops the hard ones. And then two great questions. “For what other great nation has a god so near to it as the Lord our God is whenever we call to him? And what other great nation has statutes and ordinances as just as this entire law that I am setting before you today?” The law is the sign of God's nearness. Israel's wisdom will not be its armies or its wealth; the nations will look at a people who live by God's word and say, “Surely this great nation is a wise and discerning people!” The longer reading adds a command for every Christian family: “make them known to your children and your children’s children”. June in Kerala is the month the schools reopen and the Sunday catechism classes begin a new year. Faith that is not handed on at home does not survive the second generation.

Isaiah lifts our eyes from the plains of Moab to a mountain at the end of days: “In days to come the mountain of the Lord’s house shall be established as the highest of the mountains, and shall be raised above the hills; all the nations shall stream to it.” Rivers flow down from mountains; here the nations flow up, drawn by a light. “Many peoples shall come and say, ‘Come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord, to the house of the God of Jacob; that he may teach us his ways and that we may walk in his paths.’ For out of Zion shall go forth instruction, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem.” The Church has always read this as a prophecy of Pentecost. From Jerusalem the word went out with the apostles, to Samaria, to Antioch, to Rome and, as our tradition holds, to the coasts of India with Mar Thoma. St Justin Martyr, writing in Rome in the second century, quoted this very passage and said (in substance) that from Jerusalem twelve unlearned men went out into the world and proclaimed the word of God to every race. And the fruit of that word is peace: “they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruning hooks; nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.” We have not yet seen that day in full; the news of every week tells us so. But wherever the Gospel is truly received, swords begin to become ploughs: enemies are reconciled, families make peace, communities divided by caste, language or politics learn to sit at one table. The prophet ends with an invitation, not a command: “O house of Jacob, come, let us walk in the light of the Lord!”

Paul brings the vision down to the dinner table. Corinth was full of temples, and much of the meat in the market had first been offered to idols. Some Christians said, “All things are lawful.” Paul quotes the slogan and corrects it: “but not all things are beneficial. ‘All things are lawful,’ but not all things build up. Do not seek your own advantage, but that of the other.” The question is not only what I am allowed to do, but what builds up my brother and sister. Paul is not anxious about the meat itself: “the earth and its fullness are the Lord’s.” But if someone at table says, “This has been offered in sacrifice,” then do not eat, “out of consideration for the one who informed you, and for the sake of conscience”, the other person's conscience. Love sometimes gives up what liberty allows. In our own country, where Christians live with Hindu and Muslim neighbours, share their festivals and receive their hospitality, Paul's principle is a wise guide: receive every good gift with thanksgiving and respect, never do anything that would be taken as worship of another god, and never wound the conscience of a weaker brother or sister. Then comes the sentence that turns ordinary life into liturgy: “So, whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God.” Eating, working, studying, cooking, driving the autorickshaw, answering emails: all of it can be offered. The Holy Qurbana does not end at the church door; it continues at the dinner table.

The Gospel is sharp. Jesus has been speaking about the signs of the times, and he asks: “And why do you not judge for yourselves what is right?” If you are on your way to court with an opponent, “on the way make an effort to settle the case”, before it is too late. Then some people tell him a terrible piece of news: Pilate has killed some Galileans while they were offering sacrifice, mingling their blood with the blood of their animals. Behind the report is an old assumption: those who suffer such things must have deserved them. Jesus rejects it firmly. “Do you think that because these Galileans suffered in this way they were worse sinners than all other Galileans? No, I tell you; but unless you repent, you will all perish as they did.” He adds a disaster of his own: “those eighteen who were killed when the tower of Siloam fell on them”, an accident, not a crime. Were they worse offenders? No. Jesus will not let us turn the suffering of others into a judgment on them; he turns it into a call to ourselves. When a landslide buries a village in the monsoon, or a boat overturns in the backwaters, we must not say, ‘they were punished.’ We must weep with them, help them, and ask: am I ready to meet God? The longer reading gives the other side of the picture: a fig tree that has borne no fruit for three years, an owner who says, “Cut it down!”, and a gardener who pleads, “Sir, let it alone for one more year, until I dig around it and put manure on it.” Repentance is urgent because life is short; it is possible because God is patient. The Fathers saw in the gardener Christ himself, who intercedes for us and digs around our roots with his word and sacraments. Today is the year of grace. On this Sixth Sunday of the Apostles, let us walk in the light of the Lord, do everything for his glory, and turn back to him while we are still on the way.
conn: “If you love me, you will keep my commandments” (John 14:15): the law of Moses becomes, in Christ, the law of love.
“And the Word became flesh and lived among us” (John 1:14): God's nearness, which Moses praised, has a human face.
Out of Zion shall go forth instruction.
The Risen Lord: “you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the ends of the earth” (Acts 1:8).
“Blessed are the peacemakers, for they will be called children of God” (Matthew 5:9); “The effect of righteousness will be peace” (Isaiah 32:17).
Food will not bring us close to God.
Paul had already written, “‘Food will not bring us close to God.’ We are no worse off if we do not eat, and no better off if we do” (1 Corinthians 8:8).
The first preaching of Jesus: “The time is fulfilled, and the kingdom of God has come near; repent, and believe in the good news” (Mark 1:15).
“The Lord is not slow about his promise, as some think of slowness, but is patient with you, not wanting any to perish, but all to come to repentance” (2 Peter 3:9).
altar: The nations stream to the mountain of the Lord's house; every Holy Qurbana is a small fulfilment of Isaiah's vision, as people of many families, languages and histories climb the steps of the sanctuary to be taught his ways.

Whether we eat or drink, do everything for the glory of God: at this altar we eat and drink the Body and Blood of Christ for the glory of the Father, so that every meal at home may become a thanksgiving.

fathers: From Jerusalem twelve men went out into the world. They were unlearned and could not speak with eloquence, but by the power of God they proclaimed to every race of people that they had been sent by Christ to teach the word of God. And we who once killed one another now not only refuse to make war on our enemies, but gladly die confessing Christ.

The fig tree that bears no fruit is human nature; for three years the Lord sought fruit from it, before the law, under the law and under grace. The gardener who digs around the tree is the one who rebukes the barren soul, and the manure is the memory of our sins, which, laid at the roots with tears, makes the soul fruitful again.

Do you see how even eating can become an act of worship? Let the table be such that God may be glorified at it: with thanksgiving before and after, with sobriety, with a share for the poor, and with words that build up and do not wound.
magis: The commandments express the implications of belonging to God through the covenant; moral existence is a response to the Lord's loving initiative, an acknowledgement of homage and thanksgiving to God.

Injustice, excessive inequality and envy threaten peace and cause wars; insofar as people are sinners, the threat of war hangs over them, but insofar as they are united by charity, violence is overcome, and Isaiah's word is fulfilled: they shall beat their swords into plowshares.
Interior repentance is a radical reorientation of our whole life, a return to God with all our heart, an end of sin and a turning away from evil.
Some rules apply in every case: one may never do evil so that good may result; and charity always proceeds by way of respect for one's neighbour and his conscience.
Second Vatican Council, Gaudium et Spes 78
Peace is not merely the absence of war; it is rightly called an enterprise of justice and the fruit of love, and it must be built up ceaselessly.
saints: Sixth Sunday of the Apostles. In the Latin calendar, the Twelfth Sunday in Ordinary Time. In India and many other countries this Sunday is also kept as Father's Day: a day to thank God for our fathers, living and dead.

Mon 21: St Aloysius Gonzaga (listed). Tue 22: Sts John Fisher and Thomas More, martyrs. Thu 24: the Birth of John the Baptist. Sun 27: Seventh Sunday of the Apostles. Tue 29: Sts Peter and Paul, Apostles, a day of obligation.
2027-06-20.prayer: Lord our God, there is no other people with a God so near as you are to us whenever we call upon you. Teach us your statutes, that we may live, and help us to hand on your word to our children and our children's children. Draw all the nations to the mountain of your house, and let the word that went out from Jerusalem with the apostles make swords into ploughs in our land and in our homes. Whether we eat or drink, or whatever we do, may we do everything for your glory. Lord Jesus, patient gardener, dig around our roots and give us one more year of grace, that we may turn back to you and bear fruit. To the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit be glory for ever. Amen.

kidsaint: Dominic was an Italian boy who studied at the school of St John Bosco in Turin. On the day of his First Holy Communion, when he was seven, he wrote a promise: “Death rather than sin.” He was cheerful, he played games, he helped younger boys and he stopped fights between his friends. He did ordinary things for the glory of God. He died when he was only fourteen. Lesson: you can make everything you do, eating, playing and studying, a gift to God!

term: The Greek word used in the Gospels for repentance, as in Luke 13:3. It means more than feeling sorry: it is a change of mind and heart, a turning of the whole life back to God. Malayalam: മാനസാന്തരം, അനുതാപം.

family.explain: Isaiah saw a beautiful picture: people from every country walking up a mountain to learn God's ways. They were so full of God's peace that they melted their swords and made them into farming tools. Saint Paul says that whatever we do, eating, drinking, playing or studying, we can do it for the glory of God. And Jesus tells us to turn back to God every day. Today many families also thank God for their fathers.
family.intention: We pray for our fathers and grandfathers, living and dead, and for children starting the new school year.
family.ask: Ask: “What is one thing we can do together this week for the glory of God?”

illus: Two families in a village in Idukki had quarrelled for years over a strip of land between their houses, hardly three feet wide. The case went to court, and lawyers' fees mounted on both sides. One Sunday the elder of the two men heard the homily on the Gospel: “on the way make an effort to settle the case.” On the way home from the Qurbana he passed his neighbour's gate and, without planning it, stopped. ‘We are both getting old,’ he said. ‘Our sons will inherit this quarrel and nothing else.’ They sat on the veranda and talked until the tea went cold. A month later both families withdrew the case and planted a row of plantains on the disputed strip, to be shared. The parish priest blessed the plants at the next house blessing. ‘Isaiah said swords would become ploughs,’ he told them. ‘Here a court case has become a plantain grove.’

pm.open: Lord God, there is no people with a God as near as you are to us. Draw us now to the mountain of your house, teach us your ways, and send your Holy Spirit to turn our hearts back to you. Amen.
share: What other great nation has a god so near to it? (Deuteronomy 4:7). When have I felt God near?
They shall beat their swords into plowshares (Isaiah 2:4). Which sword in my life needs to become a plough?
Do everything for the glory of God (1 Corinthians 10:31). What ordinary task can I offer to God this week?
Unless you repent, you will all perish (Luke 13:3). What is God calling me to turn away from?
interc: For the Church in this Season of the Apostles, that from every altar the word of the Lord may go out to the nations.
For peace in the world and in our land, that swords may become ploughshares and enemies may be reconciled.
For parents and catechists beginning the new year of faith formation, that they may hand on the faith with joy.
For our fathers, living and dead, and for those who have no father to care for them.
For victims of floods, landslides and accidents in this monsoon season, and for all who help them.
pm.close: Father, you are near to all who call upon you. Make us a wise and discerning people, who live by your word, build up one another and do everything for your glory, and who turn back to you while there is still time. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear friends, on this Sixth Sunday of the Apostles, Moses asks a beautiful question: “what other great nation has a god so near to it as the Lord our God is whenever we call to him?” (Deuteronomy 4:7). God gave his commandments not to burden us but so that we might live. And he asks us to make them known to our children and our children's children.

This month our children have gone back to school and the catechism classes have begun again. Parents, you are the first teachers of the faith. Do not leave it only to the Sunday school. Pray with your children, read the Gospel with them, and let them see you live it.

Isaiah sees all the nations streaming to the mountain of the Lord, saying, “Come, let us go up… that he may teach us his ways.” The word goes out from Jerusalem, and its fruit is peace: swords become ploughshares (Isaiah 2:3–4). This happened at Pentecost, when the apostles carried the word to the nations, and it happens wherever enemies are reconciled.

Saint Paul tells us that not everything we are allowed to do builds up others. Love thinks about the other person's conscience. And he gives a rule for every day: “whether you eat or drink, or whatever you do, do everything for the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31). Our kitchen, our office and our classroom can all become places of worship.

In the Gospel, people tell Jesus about Galileans killed by Pilate and about a tower that fell and killed eighteen people. Were they worse sinners? Jesus says, “No… but unless you repent, you will all perish” (Luke 13:3). When disaster strikes others, let us not judge them; let us help them, and look into our own hearts.

And Jesus tells of a fig tree without fruit, and a gardener who says, “let it alone for one more year.” That gardener is Jesus, who pleads for us and works on our roots. Today is our year of grace. Let us turn back to him, walk in the light of the Lord, and bear fruit for his glory. Amen.
kids: Children, Isaiah dreamed of a day when people would melt their swords and make them into tools for farming. That means: stop fighting and start helping!
Saint Paul says we can do everything for God, even eating and playing. Today, say a prayer before your meal, and if you have a fight with someone, be the first to make peace!
